utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Thursday, September 3, 2009, and I greet Mr. Praljak, our accused, the Defence counsels, Mr. Stringer and everyone helping him, as well as all the people helping us around the courtroom. I think I understood that a few counsels wanted to take the floor for a number of issues, so I'll give the floor to Ms. Alaburic first.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning to you and everybody else in the courtroom. The Petkovic Defence has an oral request to make, so may I have two minutes to explain, and that request relates to the documentation and topics of the crimes committed by the BH Army against the Croats on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and specifically in the areas which we call the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in these proceedings. Thus far in the proceedings it was -- permission was not granted to discuss those topics, and the explanation given was that they are issues of quid pro quo and that the alleged crimes of the HVO can't be justified by the alleged crimes committed by the BH Army. And the Chamber refused to accept documents proving that certain individuals of the BH Army had committed crimes against the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that was something that has been the practice in this courtroom since the trial began, and on the basis of that position taken by the Trial Chamber, the Defence teams prepared their witnesses for their defence case, in line with that. In the Gotovina trial, Gotovina et al., before this Tribunal, the Trial Chamber, on the 7th of August, 2009, made a ruling by which it made it incumbent upon the Prosecution to provide the Defence teams with all the documents related to the crimes that the army of the then-Krajina, Srpska Krajina, on the territory of Croatia committed against the Croats in the period between 1991 to the beginning of Operation Storm, and that was August 1995. The Trial Chamber, in its statement of reasons said the following in item 11, and I'm going to quote in English: "[In English] The Chamber further notes that evidence showing that the alleged physical perpetrators of the crimes alleged in the indictment committed those crimes out of a motivation for revenge and retribution for the crimes committed by Serbs against Croatian civilians could be potentially relevant to the determination as to whether crimes were committed within the scope and as part of the implementation of the JCE in which the accused have allegedly participated. Such evidence may offer a reasonable alternative to the Prosecution's allegation of JCE." [Interpretation] In item 13 the Trial Chamber goes on to emphasise that existence of evidence [In English] "could be of potential support to the revenge thesis and may serve the Defence in preparing the presentation of its case." [Interpretation] Would be fundamental for the realisation of the rights to a fair trial. The Prosecution of this Tribunal did not appeal the decision taken by the Trial Chamber, and as we heard from our colleagues in the Gotovina case, the OTP started providing the Defence with that material. We feel that it is case law of this Tribunal, and on the basis of that case law, we would like to propose to the Honourable Trial Chamber to make a similar ruling in this trial and by request of the Prosecution to take from the Halilovic trial, Delic, and Hadzihasanovic trials the material and provide the Defence with all the documentations on the crimes committed against the Croats. Secondly, that if the Prosecution has in its possession documents outside those three trials dealing with the same topic, that it should also be required to provide the Defence with those documents. And thirdly, in conformity with the Trial Chamber decision taken in Gotovina, we would agree that the Prosecution is not duty-bound to provide documents mentioned in the judgements, because it is a public document and, therefore, the Defence in conformity with their rules of due diligence procedure have accessed that documentation, but that this duty applies to every other document, including those protected under Rule 70 of this Tribunal. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me give the floor to Mr. Stringer in a minute. Well, first of all, I'll give the floor to Mr. Stringer right away, and I'll consult with my colleagues later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. I don't know why we need to waste court time on this issue. It's a complicated one to say the least. We suggest the Trial Chamber order the Petkovic Defence to file a written motion. The Prosecution will respond, and the Trial Chamber can issue its ruling. Of course the Trial Chamber is not bound by any decision of another Trial Chamber. So that's how we propose to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, the Trial Chamber took due note of what you are asking, but it believes that you have to make a written submission regarding this. So please file a motion given the importance of this topic, and then the other Defence will either associate themselves with your motion or write their own motion, the Prosecution will reply and give us its point of view, its position, and the Trial Chamber will rule on this issue. Thank you. And please do this as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for that decision. We will endeavour to complete our written submission by Monday. We would just like to have the deadlines reduced for a response so that we can have the Trial Chamber's decision as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'd oppose that request. Here, how many years into this trial? There's no fair reason to minimise any time that the Prosecution is entitled to under the rules to file its response within the 14 days. So we'd oppose any shortening for this particular topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. President, I want to make sure that we're on record that we join in this request by the Petkovic team. In fact, we discussed this prior to this, and in fact the decision says nothing other than what we have been saying all along throughout this trial. So it validates, and I feel vindicated that at least one Trial Chamber has taken on board the comments that I have repeatedly made on the record in this particular case. That said, I do think that if the Prosecution in a previous case has taken a position which they believe is right and honourable as that stated by the Trial Chamber, and if this particular Prosecution takes a different point of view, I think it behooves this Trial Chamber to ask the Prosecutor himself as to what his position is, because I don't think that we can have a Prosecution in an international tribunal of this type where in one case individuals enjoy more rights than accused will enjoy in another case. The Prosecution has to speak with one voice. They have to be consistent. So while Trial Chambers may differ, the Prosecution cannot use an al a carte approach, if I may borrow one of my -- one of Mr. Stringer's comments from yesterday. So I would request that the Trial Chamber write to the -- the Prosecutor himself and ask for his position as opposed to having the Prosecution teams willy-nilly decide how they're going to handle these sorts of matters which obviously affect the rights of every single accused being tried before this institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution rejects the remarks of counsel. Every case is different. The fact that a Prosecution team might take a position in one case certainly doesn't mean that a different Prosecution team has to take the same position on an entirely different case. So I don't know again why we need to waste court time on this sort of grandstanding and speech-making. Let's just get the motion filed. We'll file a response and the Trial Chamber can rule on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's wait for the motions. Once the motions will be filed, according to the rule the Prosecution has 14 days to answer. That is the procedure, and we will stick to the procedure. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just for the record, I'd like to state that the Stojic Defence, both during its case and in proposing documents, it has put forward a series of documents along the lines proposed by the Petkovic Defence, and for that reason I would like to say that I fully agree to the proposal, and I'd like to say this in public, in open session, and I shall be sending in a written submission to that effect as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does anyone else wanted to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of General Praljak, throughout this discussion, presented material along those lines and wanted to indicate that nothing happens of its own accord, and that is why we consider that the oral motion made by our colleague Mrs. Alaburic is absolutely acceptable, and we will state our views in that regard in a written motion fully agreeing with her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for the record, on behalf of the Coric Defence we agree with what the previous Defence counsel have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the counsels took the floor, all those who wanted to take the floor, anyway. Yesterday when we were running out of time, we only had a few minutes left, a question was put to the accused by -- by Judge Trechsel, and when I read the French translation, I had a problem understanding, so I said that I would look at the transcript. The English version is also quite fuzzy, actually, so I believe the best would be for Judge Trechsel to put his question again to the witness and everything will be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have re-read the question. I agree that it is lacking clarity, and I will try to put it in a -- in as clear way as I'm able.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The background to the question are two documents, one an order given by Mate Boban and addressed both, as far as we're interested here, both to the Ministry of Defence and to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, Judge. Just for the record, perhaps, since we're onto a new day, I can say that we're talking about P05104, which is the Boban document, and then P05188, which is the subsequent order from General Praljak, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. It's very helpful, and it's only fair that you interrupt me. I have interrupted you a number of times too. So we had first this Boban order, and then we have an order signed by you, Mr. Praljak, which goes on to the operation zone, to the bodies under your command. You have told us that you handed on the order by Mr. Boban not in its entirety but excluding, in particular, the third point which refers to prisoners, yet you have attached the Boban order in its entirety to your order. You have not redacted it. And in your own order you have made specific comments on, at least, number 5 of Boban's order but not any others. So if you say that you did not hand on the order number 3, this is something which we cannot verify at the -- on the documents. The documents do not show this. I have interpreted you, understood you as telling us, "Although I have handed on the full order by Mate Boban, as a matter of course, because of the limitations of the competencies of the army, I did not really hand on the order to the extent that it relates to prisoners," and I think one must also assume that it is your view that those who received your order together with that of Mate Boban understood that number 3 is not for them. So it was implicitly excluded. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Might I just add. In item 1 I say to inform -- be informed of the contents of the Boban order. So I considered it then to be proper for me to leave the Boban order as it was so that people could get to know about its contents, could become informed of its contents, but in my order, in item 3 I say -- and we're dealing with items 5 and 6 which means to enable and so on and so on as it says in item 5 and 6, and in that respect the officials might -- must be informed in writing of their assignments before being sent on duty. So to read the Boban order as it was written, and in my order taking from the Boban order that portion that relates to the army. And as far as I understood what you have just said, you have interpreted that correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For everyone in the courtroom, I'd like to draw your attention to 3D000915. That is a document from the state archives of Croatia from which it is evident that there was another order which contains and which was -- to which the Boban order was added. This order was send by General Praljak, and from that we can see, because there was a question raised yesterday as to whether Mate Boban's order existed attached to the Slobodan Praljak order. Now, everybody in the courtroom can verify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Pinter, we do not have this document before us. I think it is a befitting document for redirect, the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's fine, but I just wanted to clear the situation up now when we're discussing the matter and not have to come back to it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, we -- oh, I accept your good intention, thank you, but I think we should now give the floor back to Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, a question. I thank my fellow Judge for this question, which was perfectly clear, and I fully understood your answer also. Therefore, I have no specific problems with this issue any more. But while listening to you, this is what I understand: Mate Boban draws up an order that you receive, and you relay this order as well as your own order. You transmit these two orders. And normally on lower echelons, the people are supposed to read all documents that they receive. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in your own order, why is it that in item 5 you say that the commanders who were directly subordinated are directly responsible for carrying out this order that you just issued? Does this mean that since Mr. Boban is the supreme commander he could also directly contact the brigade commanders, or was he supposed to go through the chain of command at all times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The supreme commander can issue an order directly to the brigades, but it is customary that it goes down the chain of command, that he issues the order to the Main Staff, and then the Main Staff to the operative zones, the operative zones down the line of the brigades, and so on and so forth; that's customary. But he does have the right to issue an order skipping military hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I've got some video footage I want to show you, and then after we look at it, I'll ask you some questions. This is P00977, for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Four of them were shot. On 31st, they were hungry, they were thirsty, and they had to survive --"

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's start it over again from the beginning and maybe we can get more interpretation. I believe the text is in the booths.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you. We found the text.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] ... north of Mostar in Muslim zone. Earlier when the people were released, the Croat captors amused themselves by forcing them to run under rifle fire. Four people got killed on that occasion. Their skinny body bear witness to the horrible treatment they underwent, and their statements reveal bestialities. Packed in warehouses, starved, unbearably thirsty, in order to survive, they had to drink their own urine. "Detention in the Dretelj and Gabela camps confirm again the daily horrors that reign in detention camps in Bosnia. According to the testimony collected by the UNHCR, they were constantly beaten or burned with cigarettes. Some of them died immediately. Croatian soldiers amused themselves by opening fire from automatic rifle on warehouses where they were kept when they were drunk. Thirty of them got wounded in that way. In addition to physical harm they were also under mental torture. They had to sing the songs that were derogatory for Muslims. UNHCR employees claimed that these people are nowadays desperate and humiliated. In the Dretelj camp there are allegedly two to two and a half thousand detainees."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, General, obviously it's for the Trial Chamber to decide whether the various allegations and things that are said about the conditions were actually true. My question is a bit different. This -- the very beginning of the text indicates -- this is from 31 August. And we know from the other evidence that there was a release of prisoners from the Dretelj camp. Now, the order from Boban here is dated 15 September 1993, which is a couple weeks after this. And this is where he's saying that the prisoners of war -- or the conditions have to be brought to accordance with international standards. General, yesterday I asked you about the Mazowiecki report, whether you were aware of that, and whether you did anything to follow up on looking into the conditions in the camps. Now, this is more media coverage. I think -- I suggest it was a fairly big, well-known media event. Did you see this sort of footage? Did you hear about the condition of these men that had been released from Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. All I can do is to repeat what I said, that on that day or I don't know when this video was taken, I wasn't watching television during those days nor did I have the time or possibility to do so. All I can say is that on the 1st of September, as far as I know, I allowed a ZDF television crew. I gave permission for them to enter a camp. Whether it was Dretelj or the other one, I don't know. Anyway, as far as I'm concerned, I did this having been requested to do so. We saw what we saw, not only here when they were exchanged but over there too. I did not know, I had no information, and I told you what my duties were under the law, rather, the provisions governing the armed forces and the situation on the battle-field at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I want to take you back, General, to your testimony in this trial from the 25th of June, 2009. And this is on page 41999 of the transcript. And you're looking at a document, and in the document Alija Izetbegovic is being asked some questions. And in the document Alija Izetbegovic denied knowing about a camp called the Pogorelica camp. And he said in the document: "I did not know of the Pogorelica camp. I heard about it in Rome when the media reported about SFOR entering the camp." Now, you commented on that statement of Izetbegovic in your testimony, General, and this is what you said. You said: "Now, how is it possible that this camp could be operating with all of these services, conducting all of these affairs, with agencies that are under Izetbegovic's control, and he not know about this camp? "It's impossible -- it's absolutely impossible --" Actually, I should -- let me correct what I just said. The question to you was: " ... how is it possible that the camp could be operating with all of these services, conducting all of these affairs, with agencies that are under Izetbegovic's control, and he not know about this camp?" That's what you were asked, General. And your answer was: "It's impossible. It's absolutely impossible. Fifty per cent of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina knew about that camp. It was almost a public secret." General, I'm going to put it to you that the same thinking applies in respect of your knowledge of the HVO camps. It was a public secret. It was a notorious public secret. Everybody knew what was going on down there with these camps; the media were all over of it. And when you claim to have no knowledge, the fact is that's not true. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer, and your comparison is not good. The time is not good. Nothing is correct, in fact. First of all, the position of Mr. Izetbegovic and my position were not the same. Mate Boban knew about Gabela. Secondly, the Pogorelica camp was not a detention camp; it was a Mujahedin camp. And that camp continued to exist after the war ended. So it was a Mujahedin camp where the al-Qaeda terrorists were trained, those very same terrorists that would go on to participate in those acts of destruction in America. There was no war at the time, and all the newspapers reported it. So first of all, my position and Mr. Izetbegovic's position is not the same. Secondly, it's not the same time period. And thirdly, Pogorelica was not a detention camp. I would not go as far as to say that Mr. Izetbegovic was aware of all the camps that the BH Army held and were -- detained Croats, and there were dozens of them, I have evidence of all that. And if you admit it into evidence you will see how many of those camps there were and how many people were killed in those camps. So your comparison is not good. The time period is not the same. And my position and Mr. Izetbegovic's position are not the same. And later on it transpired that the Dretelj camp existed in September. And as far as I was able to learn, the camps were dissolved because everybody realised what was going on in there. I think that a very small number of people knew what was going on there, and those were mostly people on the inside in the camps. They knew about that, but this was not broadcast. It's not something that you go talking to people about, about the crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But when Mate Boban ordered that the camps be brought into accordance with international standards, you personally did nothing to make that order come to pass. You did nothing to implement Boban's order on the camps; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, services have their jurisdictions, their purviews. The commander of the Main Staff couldn't do anything about it, because he was not -- he did not have the power, and it was not his duty, and he did not have all the elements that he needed to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if I recall correctly your testimony from yesterday, sir, you're telling us that you do not know who or what body did have jurisdiction. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I'm not sure what body had the jurisdiction. Well, you discussed the issue here in court, so you perhaps might want to pursue that to its conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We will. General, the next exhibit is P09258 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I would like to come back to the video briefly. Since I put questions to you for six days, if you remember, I was wondering whether I was going to put this video footage to you, and if you remember at the very beginning I put some questions to you regarding prisoners, and then when you said that it was not under your responsibility, it had nothing to do with you, I did not insist any more. I wasn't actually going to show you that video footage, but Mr. Stringer put the video to you, and you saw, you noticed that it's a programme from TV 5, which is a French-speaking station, and it's from the HTV, actually. It's a Croatian -- it's a Croatian -- it's a TV station from Croatia, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I can understand that you were on the front line and that you were not able to see that programme. I understand that. But a Croatian station shoots these -- this footage which is broadcast all over the word, because TV 5, of course, covers the entire world. Now, Croatian Information Services were looking at what was going on in the conflict, or checking the conflict. And it's just a thesis, it's my own thought, I have no certainty, I cannot make an affirmation, but I wonder if in Croatia when people saw that programme, were people not wondering - Mr. Bobetko, Susak, and others - were they not wondering, we see people who are so skinny, what happened? They're released, the reporter is explaining, they shot at them, they opened fire on them, four people were killed. And of course this is a problem. Mr. Tudjman at the time, could he have not requested through the military hierarchy of the army to see what was going on and what had happened? So my question is the following: At the time, nobody called you to tell you, We just saw a programme. Nobody called you to tell you that they had seen something like that on TV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Well, first of all, from what we've heard here in court and based on what I know, Franjo Tudjman reacted promptly. Mate Granic was dispatched and meetings were convened. People learnt about this after those images were broadcast. Well, the very next day the ZDF showed up, and they asked for permission to film it. I gave them the permission. They did some more footage, and people were astonished. I said quite clearly in the 1995 interview that I as a Croat am ashamed of it. In another interview I labelled it a crime. And then there was another reported and Vulliamy asked -- well, as a human being, not as somebody who is responsible for it, I issued a laissez-passer because I didn't want to cover anything up. On the other hand when Granic came in and so on, the services that are in charge it started doing their job, and I did my job pursuing an offensive to defend the territory night after night. So officially, and believe me, temporally in terms of -- well, what can I tell you? At that time one is involved in organising the Muslim -- the release of the Muslim wounded from East Mostar, helicopters. I don't know how to explain it, but I didn't know. I learned later on as time went by, bit by bit, but meetings were held, I think in Makarska. There was a great to-do about it, and then this whole thing started being resolved. And in the end, it was resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if I understand correctly, this is the chronology: First Tudjman noticed that, then he sent Granic there. And after that, after the arrival of Granic, a whole series of events unfolded, and you said yourself that ZDF came to ask you for an authorisation which you granted. You gave them that authorisation. Is that right? Is that the right sequence of event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, but to be quite frank, I realised later on that the HDZ people were the first -- or, rather, HZ-HB, not HDZ, that they saw that things were going on differently than they had thought. I can only tell you that I let first one and then another and yet another reporter in, and that's all. And from the 10th of September until the 15th of October, I was waging a war, again with the wounded, helicopters. Well, we have to put all the documents together, and in this respect I really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, at page 17, line 2, you said that based on what you know, Franjo Tudjman reacted promptly, Mate Granic was dispatched, and meetings were convened.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I knew -- oh, I'm sorry. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Those are the first names that you've given us in connection with this issue. I've been asking you who was responsible, who had jurisdiction. Are you telling us, General, that it was Tudjman and Granic who had jurisdiction? They seem to be the only people who were reacting to any of this.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said, sir. I said that as I learned things at a later stage and based on what I heard here in court, I said that based on what I had learned and what I have learned here in court and as the meetings went on, I realised that Tudjman responded. But I don't -- Which doesn't mean that Prlic, Stojic, etc. did not react. So please don't apply this false logic to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm simply asking you, General. Tudjman reacted; he responded. Granic, he dispatched Granic down. So what you're telling us, General, is it was Tudjman and Granic who had the authority or the obligation to deal with the problem of the camps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. I said precisely what I said, that based on my knowledge, which was mostly after the time, because at that time I was not following their movements and where they met. I realised that the response ensued after the TV cameras showed what the situation was really like. And after that time there was a general alert because everybody realised that things were going on and -- well, things that I have already given you my view of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And Tudjman had to dispatch Granic down to Herceg-Bosnia to deal with it, because neither you nor anyone else on the HZ HB political side was going to do anything to fix the camps. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to this question. I have not risen because I have thought that the questions would take a different tack. General Praljak spoke about Tudjman because His Honour Judge Antonetti asked the question about when, how, and where President Tudjman did anything, and it is really inappropriate to link this question and that answer with the actions by the Herceg-Bosna officials. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I respectfully disagree with my learned friend. It was the general here who just was talking about Tudjman and dispatching Granic. This is an appropriate follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, the Trial Chamber believes that the Prosecutor can put follow-up questions regarding the knowledge that Mr. Praljak knew about the roles that people played.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, General, in fact the camps that were closed were in fact closed because Granic and Tudjman wanted them to be closed; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I cannot agree with you. You put it to me that they dealt with it and that we didn't. If I let the reporters and TV crews in to show what's going on, then at least on the basis of my signature, you can see that I'm not trying to cover up anything and that if there's anything going on I wanted the world to know about it, and I wanted the problem to be solved. That's what I'm telling you. I also told you what I had learned at -- subsequently, even here in this court based on some testimony that the international community learnt about it, that President Tudjman learnt about it, and that efforts were made to solve it, but those efforts bypassed me because I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's look at some of your remarks made in your BBC interview. We showed you part of this yesterday when we were talking about the order to disarm the Muslims. And just for completeness, we're going to start at that point again. But we're going to let the film run longer to hear what you have to say about the issue of camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And for the record, this is the clip we showed yesterday. It's from P09258, and this is pages 8 and 9 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Interviewer: The second question is about detention centres. On 17th of July, 1993, the news about the existence of those centres was published, which provoked a lot of pressure" -- inaudible. "Praljak: Yes, it is somewhat difficult for me to talk about that, because as a Croat I feel ashamed because of the existence of such things. I am ashamed because they existed. I cannot accept that we consider that a normal thing. There has never been a war or an army which, if they had to put somebody in a detention camp, did not set up such camps. That's not unusual. You have to put your prisoners of war somewhere. If there are many of them, and Herceg-Bosna was not prepared to have prisoners of war, nor did it think that there would be a conflict with the Muslims, nobody was rationally fully prepared for it. At one point, we had to react very quickly because it was literally a matter of hours as to who would disarm whom. "If you are faced with a situation at one point in which you can either react by disarming your enemy or be disarmed and thus really lose everything - I do not think that we would recover from that so well - I'm prepared to accept responsibility for the decision to disarm them. Once it all started, there was no more trust left, and it was too dangerous to wait and risk it. So I'm prepared to take responsibility for the decision on disarming in Livno, Prozor, Vakuf, and so on, even ... but I'm not prepared to accept responsibility for what the camps looked like."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you could just give us a second, Mr. President. The intention is to continue. Okay. We're going to come back to the part that is evading us now, Mr. President. But what I'm going to do in the meantime is to move to a different BBC video where this conversation is continuing P09470.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Praljak: So when it comes to disarming, when the camps started, when people had to be put somewhere, I said as I was leaving there was a short interregnum when I was not there, I remember that I said to Mr. Bruno Stojic, who was the defence minister: 'Bruno, take good care not to do something we would be ashamed of.' He told me that as regards -- prison, the prison at Heliodrom, which was under my jurisdiction, I could be sure that they would do everything possible to prevent anything unpleasant. Of course, one -- one knew that some unpleasant things would happen, because we were not able very much to control things, although it could, and that was done there. It was not under military control, and it was simply a civilian part. That is how they were set up. Upon my return, I understood from what the people had started saying already that the camps looked bad. Fortunately, Mr. Sakota came and he used his personal authority to oppose some local bosses and ensure those people were treated like human beings. In other words, he prevented ... I think that those people were grateful, although ... I personally issued orders as regards the other one in Dretelj ... one was in Dretelj and the other in Gabela. I -- I asked that they ... "Interviewer: Could you please repeat the last part. You said that you personally" -- inaudible. "Praljak: Yes, I personally demanded that the camp in Gabela be properly organised with straw mattresses, water, bathing, food to put those people ... those camps in the kind of state required by the laws of war. In that period several news teams were waiting to be allowed to film there. Of course, one could already feel that people were afraid they would see the same thing we had seen in Serbian camps. "I ordered that the journalist teams be allowed in. After all, I, myself, have been a journalist in my previous life, and I know that whatever you do it, it's better and more correct to admit that we did it, this is what happened, this is what it looks like, we did not mean it, this was not the way we think about things. We did not wish this to be our attitude towards the Muslims. This was simply a kind of madness and a mistake which happened after many of our boys were killed in the attack on the northern camp. Many of them were butchered. The blood boils to such a point that you don't think about things enough, and then you set up a camp that you should be ashamed of as a man and as a Croat. But we can still do something about it if we say this is so. And to show this is so, we will let the journalists film what they see. And, gentlemen, let the journalists in; let them film what they see. We cannot escape is this. We did it; we are ashamed of it. But if there's anything we can do, it is to show what we did, which would be the only way to prevent it from happening again. And journalists filmed it, and we survived ... "However, I cannot accept the accusations that we or I - although I did not do it - destroyed the Old Bridge and attacked Mostar. We must really accept fact that the two camps represented an ugly stain on the face of the Croatian Defence Council and our face as a people. But what we can do is to say at least that this is so."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right, General your words here raise a number of issues I want to ask you about. General, during the very first part you said that during the disarmament process, when the camps were started, people had to be put somewhere, and you said that as you were leaving, you had a conversation with Mr. Stojic, and you told him, "Bruno, take good care not to do something we would be ashamed of." Now, General, the reason that you spoke to Bruno Stojic about this is because the defence ministry did indeed bear responsibility or some responsibility for the setting up and the treatment to be given prisoners in the camps. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, that's not what was said here, and of course what I'm saying -- well, that's correct and accurate, and I still stand by it. First of all, this is an interview, and here I'm presenting arguments, and I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... General, you're not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, please, allow me. Very well. No. So my response to you is no. It's obvious that Bruno Stojic says, according to this, well, I can't really. He says, no, Heliodrom is under mine, and the other two are not. And that means that I don't know who is in charge, who's responsible. I spoke to Bruno. He told me Heliodrom was under our control and nothing else, and this is what it says here quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So everything you've been telling us so far about responsibility of Heliodrom has not been the truth. In fact, as you have just said, you and Bruno Stojic were responsible for the Heliodrom; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not responsible for Heliodrom. But, now, whether Bruno Stojic is, well, he tells me that there -- well, under that agreement -- now, I don't know whether he was responsible or not, but based on what I am saying, it's obvious that I was not responsible. And this is the return from Boksevica, so this is an interview with the man who is going back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what you said here is in fact that: "As regards our prison at Heliodrom which was under my jurisdiction, I could be sure that they would do everything possible to prevent anything unpleasant." So what you're saying there, General, is, in fact, the Heliodrom was a military investigative prison of the HVO; we all know that. It was under your jurisdiction; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not under my jurisdiction. An interview of this kind where I'm asked to explain some things, where I give those explanations, well, this is not an investigation. An interview of this kind, it's not part of the court proceedings. In an interview of this kind a person says some things that might not correspond with the facts. I'm not under investigation in this interview. I'm trying to explain on behalf of everyone what happened in my opinion, and I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. You stand by what you said here in this interview.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I stand by the fact of explaining matters and not in court proceedings. The interview was not court proceedings. It was not a trial to establish what was exactly so. I'm explaining certain things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right. Are you explaining them truthfully in this interview, or are you not telling the truth to the journalist?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say in that interview am saying a vital truth, but it's possible that I don't give the factual truth. In interviews of this kind things like that are skipped over. I am talking about a vital truth, the attitude towards camps, what we should be ashamed of, do the essence of the truth. Now, the factual truth in matters of this kind you don't always say. For me to enumerate things, it's not an investigation inquiry. It's just what I think about certain matters, and those are two different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So the vital truth --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, could you show me where in the transcript it says -- the General says that Heliodrom is under his -- comes under his jurisdiction in the interview? Could you do that, please? I've been reading it, and I can't find that particular passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If counsel's looking at the English translation of P09470, and in the bottom right-hand corner you see the page numbers 1, 2, 3, and it continues, and this would be at the top of page 2, which also has a handwritten number 30 at the bottom middle part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I see that, too, please, and could you tell me what page in the Croatian text that is to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's just play the video again. You can listen to yourself say it again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Praljak: When the camps started, when people had to be put somewhere, I said I was leaving - there was a short interregnum when I was there - I remember that I said to Mr. Bruno Stojic, who was the Defence minister, I said: 'Bruno, take good care not to do something we would be ashamed of.' He told me that as regards our prison at Heliodrom which was under my jurisdiction I could be sure they would do everything possible to prevent anything unpleasant. Of course one knew that some unpleasant things would happen, but we were not able very much to control things, although it could ... and what was down there was not under military control. It was simply a civilian part. That is how they were set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So here on Heliodrom, General, you're talking about a conversation with Bruno Stojic that took place during this disarmament process when the camps started. You make a reference to a short interregnum, and in terms of the time-frame, General, let me suggest to you that this interregnum is the period beginning on -- around the 11th of July, 1993. We talked about that the other day. When you left Boksevica, you came down to Mostar. You met with Mr. Boban. You had lunch, I think, with General Petkovic. You took a bath and may have spent the night at Bruno Stojic's. This would have been around the 11th of July, just as the arrests, the disarming was taking place. And then you left and stayed gone until the 24th of July, when you came back to take command of the Main Staff. So the interregnum period here where you're having this conversation with Bruno Stojic would have been around the 11th of July, correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but I don't think we've clarified the position of the Prosecution with respect to the objection made by my colleague Mrs. Nika Pinter on the contents of this interview. And now comparing the Croatian version and the English version and what we heard said on the tape, I can see that it was taken down from the tape wrongly, because General Praljak in this video was actually quoting Mr. Bruno Stojic, who said, "Don't worry. At Heliodrom this won't happen because Heliodrom is under my jurisdiction." But those words were not written down as reported speech in the transcript -- or, rather, as being Bruno Stojic's -- in direct speech. So that from what is lacking in this transcript, it came out as Heliodrom being under the authority of Slobodan Praljak, which is not correct, and so the transcript is not a correct representation of what was said on the tape and that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I'd like to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm sure he says that's true now that he's been fed that answer by General Petkovic's counsel. Now we've played this video twice for the General, and he said that he was giving the virtual truth even if he wasn't giving the factual truth. He's had two opportunities to clarify or to take back the words that are attributed to him. And so I think what is happening here is improper.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, would you now compare the Croatian version -- just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer could not hear what was said because he does not understand Croatian. All he could do was follow the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you all know Croatian well enough for us to be able to compare the Croatian and English text. In page 1 of pages 8 in the Croatian text at the very beginning, in the upper corner says: "When it comes to disarmament," and the English text that we had is page 30 in the middle --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that we don't have that portion of the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if you look at what Bruno Stojic said -- or, rather that Praljak said -- Bruno Stojic said [overlapping speakers] [Previous translation continues] ... Just a minute, we have to clarify this Your Honours, we have to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we're going to have this discussion, we should have it out of the presence of the witness. Because what's happening here is the witness is being suggested answers and ways to evade the words that are being attributed to him in this. Let's have this discussion outside the presence of the witness, and then we can sort it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, I agree. No problem there. I don't mind us continuing without General Praljak, but I think it's very simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see the English translation is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [Previous translation continues]... from the Trial Chamber on this request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, I had noticed what was said; of course it didn't escape. Me the question is to know who is saying under my jurisdiction? Is it Stojic who said that, or is it Praljak who said that? That's the whole crux of the question, and we have the answer in the interview given at the time, not in what Mr. Praljak would say today. He might very well be prompted by Ms. Alaburic, I don't know. But the answer to the question is in the video and the footage that was shot at the time. So the best is to look at the video once again, and we'll draw our own conclusions. Mr. Stringer, could we please play the footage once again, and then we'll see what Mr. Praljak is saying in Croat. This will be translated by the interpreters' booth. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nika, ask for a new interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, please leave the courtroom for a few minutes where you can rest a little bit, but of course you're supposed to stay in the grounds, on the premises, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we'll take a look at the footage once again in the meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may. If I may be allowed to react to what we have heard. I can't help noticing that there are, in fact, differences in the transcripts. The Croatian transcript, as Ms. Alaburic says, presents the words of -- the words as from "Sto se tice ovog naseg zatvora koji ja imam pod inerencijom," which is himself saying that he has the authority. This is, of course, only a transcript, and the person transcribing this has put in the quotation marks. The quotation marks are not in the interview, and it may be delicate to find out whether -- whether this quotation mark corresponds to what Mr. Praljak is actually saying there, and perhaps we should listen -- all listen to it in Croatian also, because that might give us an idea of whether it is convincing to have the quotation marks or not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] When -- about disarmament, when the camps came into being, I know that I was leaving. It was the interregnum when I wasn't down there. And I remember that I said to Bruno Stojic, who was Defence minister, I said: Bruno take great care. Don't do something that we're going to be ashamed of. And he said to me, As far as this prison of ours is concerned that I have authority over, you can be sure that we'll do everything to avoid any ugly things happening. Of course it's obvious to everyone that there are bound to be some bad things because our powers of control weren't that too grate. But we could do something, whereas down there it wasn't under military control; it was the civilian part. That's how they were set up. Now, when I went back down there I understood from everything that was being said - and it was being said that those camps --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when Mr. Praljak comes back into the courtroom, and he asked where this portion was in the Croatian translation, I propose that we give him that page, we provide him with the page. We've identified it. So give him the Croatian version. Perhaps you're going to say that I'm testifying now, but what he said -- and it's my mother tongue. There's no doubt. There's no doubt about it, and this discussion does not hold water. It is clear in that sentence that Praljak says, "Bruno told me that," and that's how it's been transcribed in the transcript. That's what it says. That whole sentence is under quotation marks. And there's absolutely no doubt, not the least bit of doubt, no shred of doubt.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. Now, Croatian is also my mother tongue, and I absolutely cannot see clearly that there should be quotation marks there. I consider that the English translation is good, that it's been well-translated, because when Mr. Praljak says, "I told him," and then he quotes what he told him, and further on the text there's no quotation, and further on when he speaks about prisons under military control and those not under military control, I consider that the military text is correct. And ultimately let's ask Mr. Praljak what he thinks and who said under -- in quotation marks, "our control." If Mr. Stojic used the word "our," then it meant Praljak's and his own. Or did Praljak say under quotation marks "our"? But let us ask Mr. Praljak and allow him tell us what he means. And I consider that the English translation is wholly correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to add something on the transcript. In the French translation the interpreter who translates from Croatian directly into French without going into -- through the English booth says the following, says, Stojic is talking about "our prisons." This is what Stojic told the -- General Praljak, but then General Praljak says, "our prison which is under my jurisdiction." So in the French translation, the French interpretation, Mr. Praljak does recognise that the prison is under his own jurisdiction. This is what we get from the French booth. For what it's worth, that is exactly the words we get from the interpreter. Mr. Stringer, could we ask Mr. Praljak to come back into the courtroom. You asked him to be sent out for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just before that, and I wish I could say I speak Croatian, so that I could give my opinion, but of course, I'm in the hands of the interpreters and everyone else. And maybe it's inappropriate to suggest this, but I don't whether the interpreters or the CLSS can -- as sort of a neutral party is in a position -- it may be clear from the way he's speaking, the tone of his voice, the inflection, I don't know. All I have is -- is a translation that's in front of me, and it's one that we double checked before we came into court today. I can assure the Trial Chamber that, because these are important matters. You know, whether the interpreters see this as something that is not controversial, it might be useful to know, but I don't know whether it's appropriate to put them in the hot-seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber fully agrees with this idea and is asking the Registry to please ask the competent services to translate the words uttered by Mr. Praljak during this interview in this video footage we just saw. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the record I wanted to say that I completely, wholly agree with the these -- this suggestion. We have the Croatian on the tape. It's a very good -- a very good quality. We can hear it well. And we have the written transcription in Croatian, which our opinion is absolutely correct. It's been taken down absolutely correctly. So if we have three professional translators or interpreters, and if they listen to those couple of sentences we'll get a definitive answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but I'd like to say that we agree absolutely with that proposal, and we shall accept a definitive, professional answer by the translators, interpreters, having listened to the tapes and looked through the material again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for once everyone agrees and we can only be very happy about this. Shall we bring Mr. Praljak back into courtroom? Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm just going to move -- I'm going to pass that, pass over this -- [French on English channel]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the Prosecutor is going to move on to another topic, but let me tell you, while you were gone the Trial Chamber asked the CLSS to give us a full translation of what you said during that interview. Mr. Stringer, we have ten minutes left before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may add a point. I think we need not just the translation, but also a new transcription to see whether they hear the quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may pipe in a little bit. The best evidence is what he uttered, not what's written down, and if -- in -- my respectful submission is rather than having them write some dissertation on what they interpret is for them come here and then -- or from the booth, and they can utter to us exactly their interpretation, because they're listening. This is not a written text. This is an oral text. So the best evidence is what was uttered through the witness's mouth at the time, and they can discern exactly what was meant based on the inflections. That's how it -- at least in the common law practice, that's how it would be handled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I believe the translation service will listen to the tape, and they will translate. There's B/C/S; there 's English. So I believe that more than one translator or interpreter is going to take a look at this. Normally that's the way it should be, anyway. Let's see what happens. Let's wait and see. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I want to -- I want to talk about -- well, I just want to continue, actually, from where I think I was when we -- we got side-tracked. Without talking about the conversation itself with Stojic and who said what, I was asking you about the time-frame on the short interregnum that you made a reference to here. When you were leaving, it was during this disarmament process when the camp started, and you were not there, and so I was suggesting to you, General, that that interregnum period would have been sometime around the 11th of July, 1993, when you'd left Boksevica, spent some time with Mr. Stojic, took a bath, and then went back to Zagreb. Would that be the time-frame of this conversation that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm mentioning the time-frame, the period of time, but an interregnum is something else. That could indicate something with respect to duties. I was at Boksevica, and on the 11th I think I set out for Zagreb after I had a bath at Mr. Stojic's, had dinner, and I returned on the 24th. So as to where I was when -- and we know what I was doing up at Boksevica and what I did after the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But it just seems to me, General, that you're talking about the disarmament process, which we know began in early July 1993. You say when the camp started, you said, I quote: "I said as I was leaving there was a short interregnum when I was not there." General, I'm suggesting to you that that period of time when you were not there is this period from about the 11th of July to the 24th of July. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that I wasn't there, but not as an interregnum or not having authority. Now, let me add. In this interview I'm being asked -- or, rather, I'm explaining, I'm putting forward my moral position. It is not a factual recounting but an expression of a moral position, of a possible explanation of what it was like, so that's the kind of interview it was, where what was asked for was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then I'm going to move down a little bit in the text. You say: "Upon my return, I understood from what the people had started saying already that the camps looked bad." Now, General, this would be the 24th of July, 1993, when you took command, and what you're telling us here, General, is in fact even upon your return you had knowledge that things were not proper in those camps that you discussed with Stojic before you left. Isn't that true? Or at least one camp.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, Mr. Stringer. If you look at what it says later on, I don't say after my return -- well, you know what I said. And I go on to say that I allowed the journalists through. Then we learnt that -- and I think I remember after seeing this text appear in Globus, I called up someone in Capljina because they needed blankets. And I rang them up and said, Take them some blankets. I can't remember now exactly. But anyway after my return does not mean the next day, tomorrow. It means --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the journalists were allowed through. We had to show them regardless. And I think if the translation is a good one, then apart from making possible factual mistakes, because I wasn't asked that then or did I know about all the facts at the time over there, I'm explaining my position around all this here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you said here: "I personally issued orders as regards the other one, in Dretelj. One was in Dretelj, and the other in Gabela. I asked that they --" and then the interviewer interrupted you. And you said, "Yes. I personally demanded that the camp in Gabela be properly organised with straw mattresses, water, bathing, et cetera. Those camps in that kind of state required by the laws of war. In that period several new teams were waiting to be allowed to film there. Of course, one could already feel that people were afraid that they would see the same things there that we had seen in Serbian camps." So, General, despite what you have been telling us in your testimony, what you're saying here is that you were aware that the situation, the conditions in Gabela were not in accordance with the standards and that you issued orders for Gabela to be brought up to standards. True?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, your interpretation isn't correct. If you were watching the footage, when he asked me -- I can't remember. Gabela. Well, oral speech and the transcription of speech are two different things, and if you look at the image, I'm trying to remember whether it was Gabela or Dretelj, because I don't know that at that point in time. Possibly I did, but only after information received from the journalists about what had happened in Gabela, what was going on in Gabela.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Well, actually what's indicated here is you ordered them to clean up the camp because there were news teams waiting to be allowed to get in. So you ordered the camp to be cleaned up so that the media wouldn't see what was really going on in there. Isn't that how it was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. You will see from Mrs. Ivanisevic's testimony that she called me in Citluk and that I faxed back the approval which worked. And she was able to go into the camp. I couldn't say anything to the effect, Clean it up, newspaper -- a team of reporters is coming in. She called me in Citluk, and I sent a fax to her. I had signed it. You will see that from her testimony. You cannot interpret this interview as containing the accurate fact, precise facts. You can see that I'm rubbing my forehead trying to remember what the camps are called. In this interview, I'm just trying to explain what had been going on, and I'm also making clear what my attitude is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Last question before the break. So, General, when you said in this interview, "I personally demanded that the camp in Gabela be properly organised," are you telling us that you were not telling the truth in that interview, that that's false?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, neither is true. I'm telling you that it's possible -- well, I remembered at the time probably. I can't remember now. It's possible that I demanded from the Capljina barracks to send some mattresses, but after the newspapers showed what the situation was like. Well, not newspapers, but it was the Globus magazine. Five or six days or six or seven days after the journalists had been there, I saw it, and that's what I said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time for the break. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're back in session. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I want to now move over to the second bit of BBC video of an interview that -- the part we weren't able to bring up before. And this is a continuation of the part we showed you yesterday when you were talking about disarming. And so we're going to play more of it now, although we're not going to start again at the very beginning. And this is P09258. This is bottom of page 8 of the English, and I believe that we are somewhere on page 11 of the translation, the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] You have to react very quickly, because it was literally a matter of hours as to who would disarm whom. "And if you are faced with a situation in which you can either react by disarming your enemy or be disarmed and thus really lose everything, I do not think that we would recover from that so well. I'm prepared to accept responsibility for the decision to disarm them, once it all started, because there was no more trust left, and it was much too dangerous to wait and risk it. So I'm prepared to take responsibility for the decision on disarming in Livno, Prozor, Vakuf, and so on, even ... but I'm not prepared to accept responsibility for what the camps looked like. And I would like to stress another thing here; unfortunately, it was not the army who ran those camps. The army had a prison. Let us not use that ugly word "camp." A prison at Heliodrom. And that prison on was checked by the international and humanitarian organisations within acceptable limits, give or take some problems, and it satisfied the required conditions. Let us be realistic: Of course there were incident there, that is for sure. People were beaten and so on. One could not expect us to have enough strength to organise everything in such tumultuous times. However, whatever we could, we tried to prevent and did prevent, but" -- inaudible. "And I don't know, obviously some things that were not good happened there so that the camp looked like ... at the moment I went there, and I was missing there. We should check the dates. But when I got there I did everything, and I demanded that the camps be brought in the condition that is required by the international laws of war, that reporters -- reporters be allowed in even though they looked bad, because it was worse not to let them in, because the conditions, however bad, could not be as bad as what they could depict it if you did not let them in. I demanded that the journalist teams be allowed in even though I knew, and we had to accept this because this is how it was, that the journalists would report it and that we would have to pay a price, but also that we would resolve it faster that way under pressure from the international public and by ourselves, I think that it was then resolved. Of course, I cannot justify what happened, but whatever I could do or we could do from the military side, we did. I think that you should look for those responsible outside the army. "Reporter: Did you visit any of they centres?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The tape is hardly audible.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Praljak: No I visited Heliodrom, and it looked all right. I went down there, when they told me I was to be frank, the danger of losing territories of an escalation of the war was so great that I decided -- that I dedicated most of my time to the war. I've already said something about this question. I could have dedicated myself to the camps, which would have solved the problem faster, but I would have lost territory. Where would we be there?"

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General, yesterday under oath you told us that you never went to the Heliodrom in 1993, that you were only there once in 1992 during the summer. Does this refresh your recollection, General, that, in fact, you did visit the Heliodrom and found that, in your view, it looked to be okay?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I stand by the fact that I did not go to Heliodrom. And let me repeat here, it's a TV programme called "The Death of Yugoslavia." I was told I would be speaking about general issues, and I'm here speaking on behalf. I'm trying to explain on behalf of everyone in a way acting as a front. I'm trying to explain how I -- how I understood the situation subsequently. I was not in Heliodrom in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So when you said -- because you're talking about Heliodrom. You're talking about other camps. And so when you said here that you visited the Heliodrom and it looked all right, you were not being truthful with the journalist who was interviewing you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. An objection to the question. Based on what we saw, Mr. Praljak said that Heliodrom was a military investigative prison. He didn't say it was a camp. And now in this question it is being put to him -- well, the question is from Heliodrom and other camps, as if Mr. Praljak had said that Heliodrom was also a camp. So I have an objection as to the precision of the wording, because we've all seen how Mr. Praljak described Heliodrom in his interview.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot deny what is indicated here as my words, but I don't say the year at the time. I was not in Heliodrom in 1993, not at a single point in time. You can go through my stay there from the 24th of September day by day following my stay there through orders and various combat actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You know, we can start this over from the very beginning, which we played yesterday and earlier --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- because this all begins with a question about detention centres, and then the reporter, the interviewer, makes a reference to 17 July 1993, news about the existence of these centres is published, and then you go on talking about the decision on disarming the Muslims. So clearly the whole context of this is that you're talking about the HVO, ABiH conflict during 1993. Isn't that true? You're not talking about 1992 here.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, here I use the pronoun "we," so my subsequent knowledge about something -- he's asking me what I know about that, and I explain to him that given the situation, the escalation of hatred and of conflict -- well, what is said here? And I say at one point to the journalist, one should determine the dates exactly, which means that I don't know the dates --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I'm saying, well, I'm not under investigation. I'm not presenting facts. I'm trying to explain the sense of it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, you say here: "The army had a prison. Let us not use the ugly word 'camp,' a prison at Heliodrom." All right? The army had a prison at Heliodrom. Now, General, what you're telling us here, in fact, that the Heliodrom prison was within the competence of the army; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. That's not correct. The term "army," well, when I use it, I mean the extended meaning of the term, because who was in charge in Gabela and down there, well, I don't think that it has been ascertained. You should have started from the bottom and go up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's start at the top and work down. Let's stay with Heliodrom. You're talking about the extended --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you might as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The extended army, are you making a reference here to perhaps the military police? The military police had a prison at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a military investigative prison, sir, has its explanation. Who, how, what, where? When I say the army, I mean the military investigative prison. It's part of that organisation, not -- it is not under the Main Staff. So let me repeat. It's not under the Main Staff, but I can't really tell you under whom it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, tell the truth. Stop protecting your colleagues. Tell us the truth. What part of the army was responsible for the military investigative prison at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I'm not protecting anyone. You've seen me use the term "we" in a way assuming some distant moral guilt for everything that happened. I explain what the situation was like. I'm saying that I'm ashamed as a human being, as a Croat, in any which way you like. I'm not protecting anyone, but protecting someone and accusing someone on the basis of unverified facts or facts that you're not certain of, these are two different things. In this interview I'm completely truthful, fair, and I stand by what I said there. Now you're asking me to assist you with your job and to accuse my colleagues based on facts that I'm not sure about. I was the commander of the Main Staff. I am responsible for my acts, my documents before this Tribunal. And please show me what you want to show me, and then I will tell you what I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer to the Judges and to you to the questions that you ask me to the best of my knowledge without trying to protect anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When you said the army had a prison at Heliodrom, you tell us, then, what you had in mind. What part of the army had a prison at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military investigative prison is part of the army. Now, who appoints the warden? Who at what time? Well, I don't know for God's sake, Mr. Stringer. You do understand what "I don't know" means, but I do know that it was not the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to move down to the last sentence before the next question from the reporter. You say: "I think that you should look for those responsible outside the army." Now, here, this is the bottom. I think you're --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying a little bit. I'm saying unqualified. "You should." You can play it again and you will then hear what I said precisely. I did not say "You should look a little bit for those responsible outside of us," I mean the defence system, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Maybe we had a little misunderstanding or there was an interpretation issue. I think - you can correct me if I'm wrong - you're referring to Dretelj and Gabela here, and for those who say -- "I think that you should look for those responsible outside the army." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please play this bit again? I need to look at it again, because it appears to me that I did not say "a little bit." We need to replay it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Secondly, I really don't know, bad things obviously happened there so that that camp looked ... at the moment I went there, because I was missing there for a while, you should check the dates precisely, as soon as I arrived there I did everything, and I demanded that everything be -- possible be done to put the camps in the kind of condition required by international laws of war, that reporters be allowed in even though they looked bad."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. General, maybe it would be easier for us just to walk through this. And then we'll play all the rest of it. So on this part that you've just talked about, General, again you're making a reference to the fact that you'd been away for a while, and then you returned, and you said: "At the moment I went back there, I had again been absent for a while. I should check the dates precisely.
