As soon as I arrived there, I did everything, and I demanded that everything possible be done to put the camps in the kind of condition required by international laws of war ..." Now, General, again, I'm going to put it to you, what you're saying here is that when you arrived on the 24th of July to take command of the HVO Main Staff you knew the situation of the camps, and you're claiming here that you demanded that they be put into proper condition. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the time when I went down there, when I arrived, when I was missing from that area for a while, that means that I was in a war, I was fighting. And now I said we should check the dates. I'm telling the journalist I don't have the dates at my fingertips. I don't have the facts of that kind at my fingertips. This is not the subject of this interview. I was in Vakuf. I was trying to let the convoy go through. There was some fighting. This is what I mean when I say I was missing from this area. And then the journalists came, so we're trying to determine dates here, while in the interview I'm talking about completely different things. So don't try -- because I say to the journalist, "We should determine the dates exactly."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Well --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And now you are drawing some totally --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. If you refer to the reporters, then, I know that you've talked about the reporter that came to you on, I believe, the 5th of September. So is that the time-frame you're talking about here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. On the 1st of September I got a call from a representative of the ZDF team in Capljina -- from Capljina. She called me in Citluk, and I faxed the approval from Citluk to her. I think that on the 4th or on the 5th a journalist from Globus came. On the 9th Vulliamy came. I think we all heard about that. My position is quite clear. Let the journalists in, let them see, and then do everything. So please don't now confuse some knowledge that was based on subsequent facts with those facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the approval that you issued from Citluk related to the Dretelj camp, granting access to the Dretelj camp, or facility.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir, whether it was Dretelj or Gabela. We have a statement by Ms. Ivanisevic. You can call her, the Trial Chamber can call her, and let her explain how this conversation proceeded and the approval and so on, everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, when you said here that the camps or the facilities were something for the Croat people to be ashamed of, are you referring to the Dretelj and Gabela facilities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I said that I as a Croat was ashamed. I was talking about myself, and I was referring to the fact that I saw up until 1995 -- not 1993 but until 1995. Up until 1995 I managed to learn some things. And in this interview, I claim that as a Croat and as a human being I was ashamed of all those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then when you say that in terms of those responsible, you said: "I think you should look for those responsible outside the army." Who were you referring to then, the people outside the army who are responsible?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To look for something means that that's what you do. You look for something, to seek. And it follows from this that the army was not responsible, and you should go and look for who is responsible outside of it. It's up to the investigative organs to do that. It's not my job.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I waited for the question to finish. My learned friend started replaying the videotape -- perhaps -- well, I'm insisting on it to be replayed because we have a mistake, because the English version states to look for someone outside of the army. And in the Croatian version you can hear that Praljak says, "You can look for those responsible outside of us." The word "army" is not used. So this is a discrepancy between the original and the translation, but we should listen to it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We'll play the rest it have now through to the end, and this part counsel has just referred to is at the end.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Because it's worse not to let the journalists in because the conditions, however bad, could not be as bad as what they could write if you did not let them in. I demanded that the journalist teams be allowed in even though I knew, and we had to accept this because that is how it was, that the journalists would report it and that we would have to pay a price, but also that we would resolve it faster that way under pressure from the international public and by ourselves. I think that it was then resolved. Of course, I wouldn't want to justify everything that happened, but whatever I could do or we could do from the military side, we did. I think that you should look a little bit for those responsible outside of us."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it does say "a little bit outside of us," but it's a difference between speech and written text. When I say, "Well, the army did something, but look for those responsible a little bit outside of us," it's a difference between the subtlety of speech and the cold nature of language, and that's why every text must always be authorised and that's always a problem with the transcripts and the intonation. When I say "a little bit outside of us," it's quite clear, but unfortunately those who don't speak Croatian can't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've completed my questions on this videotape, so we can move on unless there is something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In fact, I have a few technical questions regarding the video. I noticed that your watch was showing five to 12.00. Do you remember if the interview started at that time? When did it start? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was in day time. Unfortunately, they came with a bad camera and with a microphone that was turned towards me and you could hardly hear the reporter. It was in day time. That's what I'm sure, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, but I can't really tell you the exact time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have seen this footage. Do you believe that it faithfully reflects everything that you said, or did they edit it because they maybe didn't want to broadcast some topics? Or is it completely as it weapon from A to Z? Is it complete?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, we spoke for a long time. I think there are at least two hours of video footage, if not more. The essence of our interview was to explain how Yugoslavia broke down. So I dealt with political sociological issues, how the war spilt over from one area to the next, how hatred escalated. The focus was not on facts, on the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When we look at the footage, we are under the impression that you are in a very small office. We see that your military jacket is hanging on a hook and the office seems small. Can you confirm that to us? Was the office indeed very small?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a very small office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were there. There was a person who was filming and the reporter putting questions. But I also noticed on a few occasions in the video you're looking at the reporter, you're looking at him, and from time to time you look somewhere else. We see your eyes move in another direction. I was just wondering if somebody else was there as well during the interview.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think that a secretary came in once or twice, and I said to her, Beti, you don't have to be here. Maybe the lighting guy. My -- I was -- the light source was behind me, so you couldn't -- you couldn't be -- you couldn't see my face unless there was some light source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, so under oath you are telling me that nobody was controlling what you were saying? Nobody was there to tell you what to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can confirm absolutely that I spoke freely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, do you still have the video on the screen in front of you? Because just to point out -- Mr. President, I know that nothing escapes you, nothing escapes our case manager either. General, are you wearing the same tie today that you were wearing in the interview?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you can see, things last. Things in my possession last for centuries, and the only difference is that I'm older and my hair is greyer. Also, I have the suit still, the one in the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to move on. I'm going to skip a few documents in the binder, and I'm going to move to the -- what I think is the second to last document, P06729, 6729. And you're going to see, General, this relates to the period of time after you had left the command of the Main Staff and had returned to Zagreb. This is a report of the SIS and military police sector, in a relation to the work of the prisoner of war shelters at Gabela and Heliodrom, and this is to Colonel Biskic personally. And, General, what's happening here, this report to Biskic, the person that's writing this report, Mr. Cvitanovic is giving this report to Biskic on the basis of a verbal order of Biskic. And on the basis of this order, he went to these two -- or these two facilities and -- to look into the situation there and then reported back to Biskic. And I'm not going to go through all of this. He talks about Gabela first of all. According to this period of time, there are about 300 POWs in each of the said facilities. There are currently 1.268 prisoners of war. All prisoners of war are persons of Muslim nationality, male. There are some of them who are under 18 and some who are older than 60. He says: "In brief personal contacts with prisoners of war, the impression is that many of them have been brought to the shelter from their homes, street, or workplaces while the rest have been captured during combat operations. "Although there are no precise numbers for these categories, the fact is that so far nothing has been done to separate, provide accommodation, and apply all other criteria to these two so-called categories of persons housed on the premises of the shelter." And he goes on talking about the conditions. Again, I'm not going to go through this. It's rather lengthy. At the Heliodrom, this is on page 5 of the English, he talks about 2.600 prisoners of war who are of the same category as the prisoners of war in the previous shelter. Now, General, if you recall from his testimony when he came and testified in this case, Marijan Biskic testified that he arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 8th of November and that General Roso gave him an assignment by which he was Roso's security assistant and assistant for military police. Now, General, I'm going to put --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection, because my learned friend Mr. Stringer didn't fully explain what the witness Marijan Biskic said. Witness Marijan Biskic said that General Roso appointed him to the post that Mr. Stringer mentioned because at that point in time a new post was being opened in the -- a new position in the defence ministry and that he stayed for two or three weeks in the Main Staff, he remained there, and once the papers were completed, he was appointed assistant minister for security. And if we're going to quote what Marijan Biskic said about his functions in Herceg-Bosna, we ought to explain this fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm looking at the transcript page 15040. Obviously the Trial Chamber can recall or will find what Biskic's position and responsibilities are. He was asked on the 5th of March, 2007, this question: "And when you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina on 8 November 1993, were you assigned to any specific duties?" And the answer is: "General Roso gave me an assignment by which I was his security assistant and assistant for the military police. He conveyed this to me orally." That's what I've got with me. The document we're looking at is from the 18th of November, so ten days after this oral appointment Biskic, by General Roso. Now, General, my question to you is this: During the entire time that you were commanding the HVO Main Staff, did you request any reports be made about conditions in Heliodrom, Dretelj, or Gabela?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, you can ask reports from people who are subordinated from you because they come up the chain of command -- or down the chain of command. So I can't ask anybody to send me reports who is not under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So it's your testimony, General, that during the time you were commander of the HVO Main Staff you did not have authority to request or to order that reports on camps or prisons be provided to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, Judge Antonetti Your Honour, I have taken a look at the image, a reflector was there because I say its reflection on one of the hangers, the coat hangers. Referring to the footage, the reflector was to the right of the camera because I saw that it was reflected, its light was reflected on the lacquered coat hanger. I apologise for that intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to the testimony of Mr. Biskic on the 5th of March, 2007. Well, let's first do this. Let's go to the next document, General, P06805. Now, this one's dated the 22nd of November, 1993, and this is from the chief of military police administration. It appears to be -- or maybe Mr. Lavric -- well, the copy is not the best. And in this -- again, this is a report on the case of prisoners of war, and I'm not going to go through all of its terms. Rather, I want to take you to the testimony of Marijan Biskic, and I'm going to put something to you, because Biskic was talking about this exhibit, and this is page 15087 of the transcript. Biskic says in regard to this exhibit, 6805, he says: "It's a document whereby the acting head of the military police administration, Mr. Lavric, is responding to an order from me and the questions raised with respect to the collection centres or prisons or centres or POWs." And Biskic is asked more questions about the document. And then he's asked on page 15088: "Now, Mr. Biskic as a result of this initial information that you received in November 1993, what steps, if any, did you take with respect to the collection centres or centres for prisoners of war on the territory of Herceg-Bosna?" And he says: "Well, I've already mentioned that once the first information was received, I informed Minister Jukic, and the Chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council, General Roso. The result of that report was that General Roso issued an order disallowing any detainees to be taken out and saying that they should be returned. And Mr. Jukic issued an order or gave a task to the other -- to the assistant minister for the sector of health, telling him to establish a team of physicians to visit all the collection centres -- or, rather, the places where detainees were being held." And I'm going to skip a couple lines. He says: "At the same type, I proposed that these problems that were noted should be resolved, and this I did at the meetings held in the Main Staff and the Ministry of Defence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna." Now, General, here we are about two weeks after you've left the HVO Main Staff. And what we see, General, first of all, is that there are strong efforts being made to report the situation on the camps. Those reports are going right up to the Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, General Roso. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're going back to the same thing, that it says what it says there. I wasn't there any more. And it says this about Roso, although to be quite frank, from what I have seen, 80 per cent of the situations had already been resolved while I was listening and while I -- when they arrived in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The fact is, General, that within two weeks after replacing you, General Roso and the people he put in place knew infinitely more about the conditions and the situation on the camps than you ever did. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't believe they knew more, and I don't think they dealt with things like that. These are papers. You have to see who actually did what and not to see whether somebody wrote down some papers in haste and appointed someone but what these people actually did afterwards, on what grounds, and how successful they were in doing what they did. It's not only a question of writing it down on a piece of paper. There was a lot of paper writing generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What Biskic says -- what Biskic says is that these were discussed at the Main Staff and the Ministry of Defence. And the fact is that's because the Main Staff and the Ministry of Defence are the bodies that are responsible for these prison camps and detention facilities. Isn't that true? They're both responsible.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. What Roso and Biskic are going to do, it's up to them. It's their problem. When they're going to do, how successful they're going to be in what they do. And anyway, at that time the war -- rather, a conflict or the BH Army attack was already almost completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. It was their problem. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's move on, unless there are questions from the Trial Chamber, to the next binder. This is binder number ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I've indicated, this is the last sort of real binder --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: There's going to be some additional exhibits after this one, but it's not going to be a real binder, if I can put it that way, just a smaller collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we're going to -- we're going to now talk about -- or focus on the town of Mostar, mostly during the period time that you were commanding the HVO Main Staff, and the first exhibit would be P03983 [Realtime transcript read in error "P03893"], from the 6th of August, 1993. And what we see here, General, is Brigadier Tole, he appoints Mijo Jelic as commander of the defence of the town of Mostar. And then in item number 5 it says that the HVO Main Staff is to take over the command of the defence of Mostar. General, were you aware of this at or about the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I later became aware of this order -- or, rather, appointment, and Zarko Tole did have -- well, since I said a moment ago we had differed. Well, you couldn't have the classical form of Main Staff, all of us sitting in one place. And it's a little strange that Mijo Jelic should be appointed whereas later on in the next sentence it says the Main Staff takes this on, probably him. But anyway, it's his order, he had the right to say this, and I didn't stop it in any way. Let that be understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So we've seen earlier some documents about Mr. Jelic. He had been part of the military police structure. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the commander of the Light Assault Battalion of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So then what's happening here, General, and you will correct me if I'm wrong, the Main Staff takes over the command of the defence of Mostar, and then it places Mijo Jelic in charge of that command. Is that how this order is working?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's unclear militarily speaking. I'm reading the same thing you're reading, but the defence of the town of Mostar is in the operative zone. Mr. Mijo Jelic, and it is Brigadier Lasic who is in command, and then Tole and the Main Staff, or whatever you want to call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, actually what this tells us is the Main Staff is taking responsibility for the defence of Mostar out of the operative zone. Isn't that true? Defence of Mostar is going to be a responsibility now of the Main Staff. Isn't that what this says?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says in item 5, although judging by subsequent reports I know that that's not how things stood, but the command over that portion and the commander was Mr. Mico Lasic, and Mr. Jelic was a commander. He was a good combatant, a good organiser, and all the information I had, and Mr. Zarko Tole, obviously. That was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, then, this would suggest that at least as of this time Mr. Jelic is a direct subordinate of the Main Staff, and he's no longer a direct subordinate of the military police administration. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the sense of the command of the defence of the town, yes. In the sense of that kind of commanding, he was responsible for the operative zone regardless of what it says in item 5. I don't know. I can't really comment what Tole had in mind at the time because I wasn't there. I probably appeared on the -- or 10 or 12 days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And for the record, Mr. President, I think that the transcript is wrong. This is P03983, 3983.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit on this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this document from Tole is quite surprising for a number of reasons. Appointing the commander of the defence of the town of Mostar is a very important action. Who commanded the defence of the town of Mostar before Jelic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think there was the defence of Mostar as a separate part. The operative zone was divided into Sector South, Sector North, as far as I remember, and in command there was the commander of the operative zone, Mr. Mico Lasic, and continued to command there. Now, who were his subordinates in the individual sectors, I can't seem to remember just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say that it was the commander of the operational zone, Mr. Lasic, who was in charge. Very well. In the chain of command, this document states, and it's written down, that the Main Staff is now going to take over the command of the defence of Mostar. This is on paragraph 5. Now, in this framework what happens to Mr. Lasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that would mean that to the left of Mostar and the right of Mostar Lasic was in command and that Mijo Jelic was then responsible to the Main Staff. Now, Your Honour, it says what it says here, but it has no military logic, and I don't think it was put into practice that way. While -- why Tole write that down in that way, I don't know. It's the number three man in the hierarchy. He has the right to do that because it was under his purview, but this has no military logic. I think -- well, never mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document dates August 6, and you're the commander of HVO at the time. So how can you explain that you did not sign this document given the very important consequences this has on Mostar as far as the chain of command is concerned? Why is it that Mr. Tole decides to write this order without your knowing, because you're telling us that you were not aware of it. We're a bit surprised at this. This does back the case that you're developing, according to which there were three of you and that you had divided the geographical zones among the three of you, Tole, Petkovic, and yourself, and each of you only took care of a specific geographical zone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. Given the situation, the defence couldn't have been conducted from one place, one locality. Of the three Cs, control, command, and communication, we didn't have the levers to be able to do that in the customary way, that is to say to sit in the Main Staff, to stay there and issue orders that way. And I've explained that. So the commanders had to go into the field. I went to Gornje Vakuf; Tole was given the south. And in my view they couldn't have broken through there. And General Petkovic was supposed to continue to negotiations. I informed General Morillon that Mr. Petkovic will continue on behalf of the HVO to negotiate and that they should deal as much as possible with Kiseljak, Vares, and so on, so that we should not lose our positions up there. That's how things stood. It couldn't have been any different. Because you can't pretend you've got something if you haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This distribution of competence on the field had been done according to -- with Mate Boban's approval or without his knowing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Approval wasn't requested, and it wasn't behind his back either, without his knowing. It's his commander, his chief of Main Staff, three officers that sit down, take stock of the situation and say, "Here's what we're going to do."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next one is P04719. So now this document is a little over three weeks later in time now. This is the 1st of September, 1993. 4719. General, we looked at this one during an earlier part of your cross-examination when I was asking you about all of those units that are listed in paragraph 1. I want to move to a different part of this now. In the second section there, page 2 of the English, under the heading of "Mission." And just for the record, General, this is your order of 1st September 1993, on organisation of the command structure and offensive/defensive operations in South-east Herzegovina operative zone.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have the document. I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You recognise this as your order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I signed it. It's a document that I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, under the section on mission, item number 3 says: "Mission: To clear Mostar of MOS forces (the right bank) and in subsequent offensive operations to take control of Mostar and be Bijelo Polje." And then next is item 2. You say: "The South-east Herzegovina operative zone is to be divided into three sectors, Sector South, Sector Mostar Defence, and Sector North." So, General, before we move on, would you agree that this suggests that as of the 1st of September, 1993, among the possible goals or objectives of the HVO armed forces would be to clear the right bank of Mostar of the ABiH or MOS forces, and then subsequently through offensive operations to take control of the entire town of Mostar and Bijelo Polje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Stringer. One of the possible tasks of the HVO was that, too, a counter-offensive to capture or, rather, to rout the then- enemy of the BH Army, and to clean up Mostar of MOS forces. And that is why this word “to clean up” is always wrongly interpreted. In other words, of MOS forces. These were regular preparations for – only preparations, of course, to jolt them out of…

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was just preparation to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then we were just talking a moment ago about the Tole order appointing Jelic. Let's talk a little bit more about the Sector Mostar Defence, because moving down to paragraph 2(2), if you see that, you're describing this Sector Mostar Defence. Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you say that: "Sector Mostar Defence shall comprise the 2nd Brigade and the current complement of the Mostar defence - without 1/3 brigade." The translation is a bit unclear on this. You lay out the zone of responsibility of the Sector Mostar Defence. And then -- now at the top of page 3 of the English you say: "Commander Mijo Jelic Sector staff to be made up of the Mostar defence staff and a number of officers of the 2nd Brigade, Command post: Mostar." So, General, just now looking at this order, your order -- well, let me continue on to the next one, and then we can round it all off. If you look at the next one which is P04777, this one's dated the 3rd of September, 1993, and this is an order over the signature of Miljenko Lasic. And at the top, General, I think we can agree, General -- or General Lasic -- Colonel Lasic -- Brigadier Lasic, he's referring to your order that we just looked at. We can tell from the reference numbers. So that would you agree with me, General, if I suggested to you that in the Lasic document what we see is he is implementing your order and sending it down the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We can agree on that, but what I said earlier still stands that Miljenko Lasic is ordering. And on the 1st of September you can see that I divided the defence within the operational zone. You can see the south of Mostar, and there's no mention of the command of the Main Staff. Miljenko Lasic is the commander, and he is in command of three sectors as they have been -- had been divided up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So that was my question, to clarify what was the status or where the Mostar defence fell within the chain of command as of this period of time. So, General, are you saying that the defence of Mostar remained under the operative zone command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. You can see that from both those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But that Mijo Jelic was the commander, nonetheless, of the Mostar sector.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It says here that he's the commander of the Mostar sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So that part of the Tole order remained in effect, whereas the other part about putting the defence directly under the Main Staff seems to have been set aside.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it simply didn't function that way, and it couldn't be acceptable to me. A part of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the witness please repeat what he has just said. He's speaking much too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, you were speaking a little bit fast there, and the interpreters have asked if you could say again your last few sentences. You were saying -- you said: "Well, it simply didn't function that way, and it couldn't be acceptable to me," and then you were going on to say, "a part of the..." And that's where they lost you. I don't know if you want to continue from that part or not.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's not that I couldn't accept some things because I was not aware of Tole's -- well, I knew that he appointed me or Jelic, but that he resubordinated that to the Main Staff, I didn't know that. Well, this is how it should be in military terms, Mijo Jelic is the commander of the 1/3 of the south-eastern operational zone, and he is subordinated to Mr. Miljenko Lasic who is the commander, who is in turn subordinate to the Main Staff. That's how it was, and that's how it was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I take it, General, that as of this period of time you were satisfied with this chain of command in respect of the defence of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They didn't lose, so I had no reason to be dissatisfied by the fact that they repelled quite successfully the attacks by the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to move to the next exhibit unless there are questions. General, P04420.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this is an ECMM report that's a confidential document, Mr. President. I think we can talk about it, but it can't be shown on the screens outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, recognising that you weren't receiving these reports at the time, this is an ECMM report dated the 22nd of August, 1993. This is from the Regional Coordination Centre of the ECMM in Zenica - it's going out to Zagreb - and it regards the desperate humanitarian situation in Mostar. It says: "This regional centre has reported regularly," this is paragraph 1, "the dramatic deterioration of the humanitarian situation in the sieged part of Mostar. The Muslim east part of the city has about 55.000 persons stuck under constant fire since the 9th of May, i.e., more than 3 months, with no humanitarian convoy since the 2nd of June ..." Now, General, first of all, would you agree with the statement here that there was a dramatic deterioration of the humanitarian situation in East Mostar at this time, August 22nd, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What do you -- and what's the basis for that conclusion? Did you acquaint yourself with the facts and the conditions in East Mostar and make your own determination?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the reports and conversations with my assistant for VOS about what the situation was like on the enemy side and also the situation in general, no information to this effect had come in and -- indicating that the situation was dramatic at all. So the fact that there was shooting that started on the 5th of May, what this gentleman is writing -- well, I'm not going to say his name because he's protected. But this is just some kind of general -- well, there was no shooting of that kind at the time. He doesn't specify who attacked whom. He doesn't say what kind of weapons the BH Army has. He doesn't say that on the 30th of June -- well, you have seen here and you can look at other footage from the international organisations depicting people in East Mostar. You will see that they look quite well and they are -- they all have clothes and things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General, it says here, and this is the beginning paragraph 2, there's a reference to the convoy led by Cedric Thornberry that entered East Mostar yesterday, which would have been the 21st of August, 1993. Now, General, Mr. Thornberry came and testified in this trial. Perhaps you'll remember. The fact is that in order to reach East Mostar, Mr. Thornberry and that convoy had to get the agreement of the HVO. Isn't that true? Because it was impossible to drive into East Mostar without moving through HVO-held territory.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, convoys had HVO approval regardless of what you take the HVO to mean. The problem of convoys entering the area was caused by the aggression of the BH Army with them opening fire on the road. That's number one --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, you're not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- over a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The question was whether these convoys would have to have the approval of the HVO to enter East Mostar because they have to pass through HVO-held territory. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So in order for a humanitarian convoy to reach East Mostar, you're saying that it could drive into East Mostar without moving through any HVO-held territory?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That makes no sense. They had to pass through a territory that was not held by the HVO but by a road, and according to all the orders issued by myself, Petkovic, Mate Boban, they had every right not to be stopped. And now at times, 1 or 2 per cent of the convoys did not pass, well, we explored the issue here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But the roads they would have to use in order to cross over into East Mostar, those roads were controlled by the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The roads were controlled by the BH Army up north; and in the eastern area, they were controlled by the VRS; and to the south, on the 15th of August, they were under the control of the BH Army in Blagaj. So let's look at the maps and then we'll be able to talk. Here --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the implication seems to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So your testimony is that this convoy could have driven directly into East Mostar, all the trucks with flour and all the other goods, all of that could have driven directly into East Mostar from Jablanica without passing through any HVO-held territory or check-points. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. They could come in from Jablanica until the second -- the other part of the Bjelica Bridge was destroyed by the BH Army. This whole road was controlled by the BH Army up until the actual entrance into the town of Mostar; that's what I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then at the entrance to the town of Mostar, what happened there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What entrance, southern or northern?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Northern.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The northern part of Mostar and Bijelo Polje, too, and the Bijela Bridge, and the road to Jablanica was controlled by the BH Army. The HVO was on the other bank of the Neretva River, and the road is quite some distance away. Well, it's far away -- enough far away from those positions so that it was passable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next document is P04470. P04470. Do you recognise this document, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this is a pass that you issued to Ms. Sally Becker so that she could move across to the left bank?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, it says here, and this is 24th of August, 1993, two days after this ECMM report we just looked at. So do you remember -- did you speak to Ms. Becker personally? Did she come to you, or did you hear about her? Did others tell you she wanted this pass?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember any more to be quite frank. So many events occurred. I think I met her, but let's leave the matter open.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall if Ms. Becker ever talked to you about the humanitarian situation in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if I can't remember whether I talked to her at all, I certainly can't remember what we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever read her book that she wrote about her experiences after -- her experiences in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General, if -- if somebody could just drive right into East Mostar from Jablanica, then why did Ms. Becker have to come to you for a pass to move across HVO check-points to the left bank?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, the road from Jablanica goes through Konjic, Tarcin, Visoko. What would Sally Becker -- how would she be able to go through there? She came from Split. She wants to pull out a child; she asks. And if you want to see how a commander behaves, we say, We approve. I approve. And a commander of the Main Staff acted precisely as he should have done, whereas you're pulling sentences out of context and assuming things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm just asking you, General. She doesn't need to move through HVO check-points to get to -- well, let me -- let me clarify then. You're saying that she came from Split. So you're saying that the HVO controlled access to East Mostar from the south?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only from the south. We have lines, and the control of the road from the -- from the south was maintained by the HVO on the left-hand side; and on the right, the BH Army. You should take a map and determine the distances between the soldiers and these lines. I'm in command of the HVO soldiers, and I say, You're going to do such and such. The BH Army could have shot as they did, and the Serbs were shooting too. It was a war. We were an army first and foremost, and I'm telling my soldiers, We, as an army, are going to let through --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, we've just been talking about access to East Mostar from the north. And if I understand your testimony correctly you say that anybody could drive into East Mostar from Jablanica and that they would not have to pass through any HVO-held territory; correct? From the north.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is completely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, to come into East Mostar from the south. Are you saying that somebody could drive into East Mostar from the south and also could reach East Mostar without passing through any HVO-controlled territory?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, let's take this one by one. From Metkovic to the Croatian border, the area is controlled by Croatian forces. From there to the beginning of the Mostar valley, river valley, at Blagaj, those could have been the HVO check-points, the military police or whoever. From that point in time or from that position, from Blagaj, the 7 or 8 kilometres that are left to Mostar on the right-hand side, you have the HVO in part. On the left-hand side the BH Army, and up on the hills the Serbs or the Army of Republika Srpska. Who is going to shoot?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then 2 kilometres before you enter East Mostar, you had the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, in order to get to East Mostar from the south, one would need to pass through both HVO- and ABiH-held areas. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The road along those 2 kilometres to the entrance, just he road was controlled by the HVO. But the BH Army units - once again we need a map - were very close by the hills, the hillocks, in fact, to the right of the road leading into Mostar. And then on the higher hills was the Army of Republika Srpska and its artillery. And then 2 kilometres before you enter Mostar, the HVO stops and the BH Army starts. And I brought in the convoy up and to that point that is mentioned here with the man's name, the other convoy. Right up to the check-point, the entrance controlled by the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, let's look at more of your statements in your BBC interview. This time you're talking about Mostar.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: For the record, this is P09258. This is the beginning -- or at the bottom of page 6 of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] As far as Mostar is concerned, to be honest, if the war develops further, I had a plan how to take the left bank, although there, too, because of the enormous international pressure and the accusation that we were doing in Mostar the same thing the Serbs were doing in Sarajevo, we were forbidden to plan an operation to take Mostar in a way which would be successful. Personally, I was -- I did not deal with Mostar. "Interviewer: You said you were forbidden to do it, by whom? "Praljak: By President Tudjman. President Tudjman, in fact, asked us not to touch Mostar. We could wage war outside Mostar, but the town itself, because of pressure from international circles and the public was so huge, and they claimed -- and I think it was totally unjustified. I had to let the convoy pass. Well, that was a decision that I implemented. You see, we tried to be soldiers in the proper sense. A political decision was given absolute priority over a military decision. You cannot conduct the creation of a state from 20 different centres but from one. And the others, who have the right to ask and to comment, to suggest, must implement the decision that has been taken, regardless of whether it is against the feelings of the army at that particular moment and so on. And I think that the boys -- that the guys and I did it properly, fully aware of the fact that an order had to be carried out. In this case the order came either from Mate Boban -- well, but definitely from President Tudjman. By and large, that is. I don't want to say that he was responsible for everything that happened, but it was clearly a policy that protected overall Croatian national interests."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, during the time that you were commander of the HVO Main Staff, is it true that it was President Tudjman who was setting military policy in respect of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. You must understand this in the proper way here. I'm referring to Mate Boban and a meeting attended by Mate Boban where we -- where Franjo Tudjman was saying -- well, of course you have to understand each of the points made here; pressure from the international community; pressure on the Croats, that is; and of course on Croatia, on Franjo Tudjman, was very great. It was completely false, ill-placed, wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. We're dealing with interpretations here. If you don't want me to tell you about the facts and what this is about, if you keep interrupting and cutting me off, we'll never get anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, allow the Prosecutor to put questions to you. And if it seems that the questions should be developed, you will be able to do so, but at least let the Prosecutor put his questions, show what he wants to say, and then you can contest it if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we looked a few moments ago at your order in which it was envisioned there was preparation for eventually taking all of Mostar town. What you're telling us here is that you were never able to do that because President Tudjman would not permit that. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true. Mate Boban -- well, the strategic decisions such as an attack on Mostar. Let me go back to the order. It says there: "Prepare there and bring to me for signing." They did not prepare anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, General, General, General. You haven't read the item where I see, "Bring it to me to review and sign." So there's no plan, no insight into the general subject matter, no signature. You can't take part of an order without looking at the other part. It's preparations for -- secondly --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General, I'm going to put my questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe it's time for the break; correct? Now would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Let's take a 20-minute break, and we'll get back in this courtroom at ten to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Court a back in session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, just before the break we looked at the video-clip from P09258 on Mostar. What you said here, General, what you indicated, you made a reference to a convoy. And it is the top of page 7 of the English. General, do you have the transcript, paragraph that begins "President Tudjman asked us in fact not to touch Mostar"? Do you see that? This is top of page 7 of the English. And I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Page 8, at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And moving down a few lines you say: "At one point I had to let that convoy pass. After all, it was a decision, and I implemented it." Now, General, when you're talking about that convoy, you're talking about the convoy that we've seen in the video where you got on the tank and told people to move out of the way. Is that the convoy that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so what you're saying here is that the reason why you forcefully -- acted forcefully to get that convoy into East Mostar was not to improve the humanitarian situation there. Rather, you were doing it because you had been commanded to do it by Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Because it was in the political interests of Croatia to be seen to allow or to facilitate the movement of humanitarian aid into East Mostar. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I let the convoy pass through after the failure of a representative on international community, Mate Granic and Mr. Prlic, to do so, and then Mr. Prlic approached me and asked me, Can you do it? And I said, Well, yes, I can. Let's give it a try. Why was it so? Because, yet again, the people stopped it. It's a political problem, but you can't solve it with political issues. It's impossible to fire at people, to make them disperse, and that's why I used the -- well, made use of my ability to do it, to organise it, and to do it as quickly as possible. The convoy was allowed to pass through for humanitarian reasons, because that was also the position of the politicians and all the structures, that convoys should be allowed to pass through, that they shouldn't be stopped. And Franjo Tudjman has nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then why are you referring to President Tudjman in your interview here? You're the one who's invoking the name of President Tudjman in reference to Mostar, and I suggest to you in respect of this issue on the convoy. It was a political decision which you accepted and you implemented in order to get that convoy into East Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Franjo Tudjman is not here at all. Franjo Tudjman came into it after a meeting in Split in late October 1993. We have a transcript of that meeting which was a meeting of general nature, and now if we can talk about the political will, we can talk about Prlic's political will and my political will and the political will of some other people, but I at that time had to take part in something that was not a military issue. Passing the convoys through in Citluk, well, that's not something that the army should do. But since nobody else could do it, and Praljak, by happenstance, can do it, then Praljak will do it. That's all. So Praljak was supposed to implement the political will, but not of Franjo Tudjman but of Prlic. And he had failed to do that, but not because he didn't have the political will but because he simply didn't have the power to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And when you said here that a political decision has an absolute priority over a military decision, what you said there is that it is the duty of the military to carry out the political decisions; correct? The policies made by the politicians.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the army's not there to implement political decisions that just occur to anyone, but the political decision of Mate Boban as the supreme commander and the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna deals with strategic decisions of a military type. That's what I've already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So defence is one thing, but, for instance, the approval for a counter-offensive in Mostar, in that case the Main Staff must plan and implement it, and can do it. But it is approved by the politicians, the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And in this case, as you've said, not only Supreme Commander Boban, but it was Tudjman who prohibited, who was opposed to any operations to take Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you have to take into account the date, first of all the date. The request that -- the explanation why not did come from Franjo Tudjman. So the explanation, the insistence, the request, because the international community was pushing him, twisting his arm for no reason at all. So first of all you had the spin, the moderators of war first fabricate information, and then they twist their arm, and any attempt to say, well, this is not how it is -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And when you say at the end here that it was clearly a policy that protected overall Croatian interests, what that means is that Tudjman didn't want you to attack Mostar, East Mostar, because the international reaction would be -- would have a negative consequence for Croatia. Isn't at that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they always linked the situation in Croatia with Bosnia and Herzegovina. Because you can see as far as Mostar is concerned, to be quite frank, if the war goes on, I had a plan how to take the left bank. And then I go on to say about -- to speak about the international pressure, because in 19 -- because for the international community Uzdol, Grabovica, and the Offensive 93 did not exist. You cover up some information, you push to the front some other information, and then you twist Franjo Tudjman's hand. He comes down there begging -- and then you lose. We were the hostages of the pressure that was exerted on Croatia through us. We were hostages. We couldn't wage the war in the same way that the BH Army could because of some false reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's right, General. I think we agree on that. The military goals and objectives of the HVO were limited, and the limitations were coming from Zagreb, because, ultimately, it was Croatia's national interest that had to carry the day. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not so. When an army attacks me and wants to reach its western borders, it is a duty and the right of the commander, of the supreme commander, in every war to respond to the offensive by launching a counter-offensive, in particular, when the enemy, the enemy army, has done everything to inflict -- defeat on you. And once they lost, they were very weak, very weak. And to be quite frank, had we acted as they had, a political decision would be made, and I would have been in a position to take the east -- eastern part of Mostar. But the political decision, the request of Franjo Tudjman and the decision of Mate Boban was, No, no, don't do it. Peace. Let's have peace. Yet again, peace. And peace was always established when Muslims were losing. When they were launching an action to defeat us, then everybody just kept quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to move to the next exhibit, P10963. 10963. General, do you recall giving an interview sometime in the fall of 1993, while you were still in command of the HVO Main Staff, do you recall giving an interview to Roy Gutman? He was a writer for "Newsday," a European correspondent.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Because what you have here is the article that was published in December, on the 21st of December, 1993, by Mr. Gutman based on his trip to Mostar and a discussion with you. And I'm not going to cover all of it. He's talking about the situation in East Mostar. And at the very bottom of the first page of the original language version, and this would be toward the top of the second page of your version, General, it says: "Commander Slobodan Praljak justified the destruction of the Old Town on the grounds that Britain levelled Dresden during World War II and the United States used the atomic bomb on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. 'The Western countries have no grounds to claim moral superiority.'" Now, General, that's a quote that's attributed to you. He says he attributes to you the following, he says: "He made no apologies for severing land routes into Central Bosnia, leaving more than a million civilians in a desperate struggle against starvation and winter. 'I did it,' the Chief of Staff said in an interview shortly before he was ousted last month. 'War is war. Civil war is always a total war.'" General, are these your words, "War is war. Civil war is always a total war"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Stringer, after awhile, after some time passed, some months after I received the text from this man Gutman, I responded to him in a letter where I indicated that it is entirely incorrect, that his interpretation of my words was entirely incorrect. And I particularly remember that he attributed to me the words about the Croatian Lebensraum, which is a reminiscent of the use of the term by the Nazis. And I said that I find it strange, and it is not clear how a professional can twist my words to fit his political options. And I think that I could be even -- be able to locate my response. So at any rate, this is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Well, then, just to finish this off, and I understand that you challenge this, I'm going to move down five paragraphs to the part that you've just referred to. Gutman writes: "Praljak defended the siege of Mostar and the entire war against Muslims as a 'kampf fur Lebensraum,' German for "battle for living space," a phrase not heard in Europe since Adolf Hitler's Third Reich. He was referring to the ethnic balance caused by the flood of mainly Muslim refugees from Serb conquered Northern and Eastern Bosnia into regions Croats had dominated for centuries." So, General, I understand your position. You dispute having used the phrase "Lebensraum" in your interview with Mr. Gutman?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, when you're talking about the imbalance that was created, and what I've told you dozens of times, and when this gentleman here uses the term "Lebensraum," and when he says that this was not heard in Europe since Hitler and then he attributes this to me, I am still ashamed for this man. It makes me feel embarrassed. And I did not get a response from him. I cannot see how a journalist who won the Pulitzer Prize is able to twist somebody's words in this manner, attributing Hitler to me and Ustashas and saying that we wanted to take some areas, when what is written down there is about the minimum of the ethnic balance, which was at our detriment -- to our detriment, so please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to the next exhibit, Mr. President, unless there are any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I have a question on this document. You know, and this is no surprise to you, that I would say that when a journalist is putting something in quotation marks, it's because these words were actually said, uttered. Otherwise, this goes against the ethics of journalism. I don't know this person, Roy Gutman. You said that he was awarded a Pulitzer Prize. You're probably right. But he is putting words in your mouth. So he says that you did say a number things, and there is this so-called Nazi sentence -- phrase that is mentioned, and he puts it in quotation mark. I remember that you've lived in Germany, and you know German. So maybe because you know Germany, you know the German language, and you know German history, that might have uttered these words. But now you are under oath, and you are challenging everything that is in quotation marks in this text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We had a long conversation, a long conversation. And when out of a long conversation -- well, let me tell you. Mr. Gutman discovered Manjaca, and he won the Pulitzer Prize for that, and he is a big name in journalism. That's beyond that. So if you sit down for two hours with a journalist of his calibre and -- well, allow me to say that I know how to carry a conversation, and when he pulls out some terms -- I may have used "Lebensraum" at one point. But I provided an explanation. Not Lebensraum, we will expel the French, the Ukrainians, the Polish because we are the chosen people, well that explanation was, We are now defending the last bits and pieces of the territory that we used to have in Bosnia-Herzegovina against Serbs and Muslims alike. And here he says, Well, he used the term "Lebensraum," and a phrase that hadn't been heard since Hitler. So for God's sake, he's talking about the siege of Mostar. How can I tell him about the siege of Mostar when there was no siege of Mostar? And so on and so forth. So this is an unprofessional, an ugly thing that he did. I responded to him. I asked my daughter to translate my response into English. You can speak to her on the phone. She can come here to testify, to confirm that I said that he should be embarrassed for writing something like that, a journalist of his calibre, and I never received any answer from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Again, or still with regard to this text, it is here reported that you had compared the -- I think he says the destruction of the Old Town of Mostar with what the British had done to Dresden. Does that ring a bell? Do you think you have said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, the Spanish Battalion counted each and every shell that fell on the eastern side fired either from the Serbs or from the HVO, a total of shells that impacted there. Well, I didn't destroy Mostar. It's impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I read what Mr. Gutman wrote. It's on the first page, the last paragraph: "Commander Slobodan Praljak justified the destruction of the Old Town on the grounds that Britain levelled Dresden during World War II and the United States used the atomic bomb on Hiroshima and Nagasaki." End of my quote here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Incorrect. Incorrect. Incorrect. I probably opposed his moral superiority, and I spoke in conditional terms. I did not destroy Mostar. The smallest possible number of shells was fired on my orders. The town was not destroyed by Croats but by Serbs. You've seen the photographs. This is a lie, and it's utter nonsense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I take it that you did probably not say, "I destroyed Mostar." That, I absolutely believe you. But hypothetically, it seems to me that the comparison with Dresden or Hiroshima and Nagasaki is a bit in the line you sometimes argue here. When there's a prison, then you speak of Abu Ghraib or Guantanamo. Do you recall having made such a comparison, even hypothetically? I don't want you to admit here, Yes, I have destroyed Mostar. That's not my question. But the comparison with Dresden, Hiroshima, Nagasaki?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could have only in juxtaposition to his moralistic superiority. Those people came as if nothing else had ever happened in history. And now they suddenly appear -- and now suddenly you have these very evil Croats who are waging the first war ever, having the first conflicts ever, and I said, Well, there's -- I don't want to listen to you telling me what I should do in moral terms. So -- so I don't want him to tell me what I should do. I conducted that war in very proper terms given the situation we were in. And compared to other wars, and I'm ashamed of what happened. That one -- well, people invested a great deal of effort to reduce the quantity of things that every war brings with it, whether we wish to acknowledge that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, let's look at a bit more video. This is from P06365. This is the documentary that was made by Jeremy Bowen. I believe the record indicates that this footage is from September of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "It gets no better at night. Five hundred Muslims have just been robbed and thrown out of their homes in West Mostar by the Croats. They had to cross the river Neretva to get to comparative safety on a bridge made of rope and planks."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I may have moved a bit fast. I don't know if the interpreters had time to get the papers together, so let's start it again and maybe just to make sure the interpretation's going out for everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you give us a reference, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The reference -- well, it's P06365. It's my understanding that the specific pages are in the booths.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we have it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "It gets no better at night. Five hundred Muslims have just been robbed and thrown out of their homes in West Mostar by the Croats. They had to cross the river Neretva to get to comparative safety on a bridge made of rope and planks. Bosnian soldiers told them which way to go. The Croats were shooting at the people they just made refugees. Only a few hours before several Croat gangs had come for them and forced them over the front line. They thought they were safe. They had been settling down for the night. The Croat machine-guns didn't let up, and the refugees kept on coming. They were trying to kill old men and women, mothers and their children. She was so frightened she could barely walk, but she tried to calm her sons. Each new family has to be fed and housed. This is a war crime with a cold purpose to increase the purpose on the military authorities in East Mostar. The brutality of the expulsions drives home the message that compromise with Croat extremists is neither possible nor desirable. The refugees spent their first night in East Mostar in a bombed-out theatre. In one evening all of them had lost their homes and possessions. They took to persecution, rape, and murder. "We were driven to a small wood. My sons were pulled out of a car. They were taken into that wood. I was told their throats were slit. I only live because I have to. Only because I have to. What sort of life is this?"

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, what did you do to put an end, put a stop to the evictions of Muslims from West Mostar such as we've just seen here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, what we see here is the crossing of certain group of people, not more than ten different individuals. This story about 500, there's no -- nothing to bear that out in the document. I don't know why they were crossing. Everything that the army was supposed to do was that there were 8.000 Muslims in Mostar. Now, whether most probably there were individual expulsions, but when you have 8.000 people living in an area after an offensive and so on and so forth, that speaks of an attitude, a position, the quantity of power which is not absolute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So whether somebody from some house was -- I couldn't do anything -- yes. These were illegal actions, not planned and approved actions. I couldn't stop it because I didn't know it was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You didn't know this was happening. This is in Mostar, the Mostar defence sector that's been established under your order that we were just looking at. The fact is, General, that like the camps and like the arrests and like all the rest of it, you were fully aware that this was happening on a systematic scale in East Mostar. You just didn't care. Isn't at that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What you're saying is not true, not in any of the details or in any of the facts. Here we just have some images of a crossing. We have no proof of expulsion, no names, no nothing. And the person who came to take this intended to take footage of the BH Army. That's what he wanted to do when he came in September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I was waiting for the translation, and again and again, and I'm really embarrassed to do so so often, but I with like to ask you, Mr. Praljak, to speak slowly. Sometimes also, as I used to say, Mr. Stringer should also speak slowly, because also you are carried away with your arguments. But again and again for your interest, for both of your interests, it is really better to speak slowly and to stop at the questions and the answers, as the case may be. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Prandler, Your Honour. Please believe me when I say that I do have your words in my head, but then my thoughts run away with me and I speed up. I've already been here 52 days, so -- and then when you hear things that you don't agree with, it's difficult. I can't separate my emotions and my body from the rational. Unfortunately, I can't do that. That's just not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to move to the next exhibit. In the binder, General, it's P04495. General, this is a report dated the 25th of August, 1993, from Mladen Knezovic, mixed-rocket artillery regiment, Siroki Brijeg, reporting to the Main Staff. And right at the beginning there it says: "Combat operations. "From the early morning hours of the preceding day, fire was directed at targets in Mostar. Intensive operations against targets in Mostar lasted until 1500 hours. T" -- It says "T-30." I think that should be "T-130 tanks were primarily used to fire from several firing positions." And it goes on to describe more about this. General, is it correct that reports were issued by the appropriate units to the Main Staff regarding their use of artillery and firing at targets in Mostar? This was an issue that was among the reports that were sent to Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a period of time, and that mostly stayed with the operative zone, but then the number of -- amount of ammunition would be for 10 days, 15 days. You would have different reports about the amount of ammunition used, and that reached the Main Staff, too, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was it the Main Staff, then, that would have to coordinate the amounts of ammunition, allocate amounts of ammunition, that sort of thing, to determine where the ammunition would be used, how it would be used?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the artillery of the Main Staff controlled the amount of ammunition used, how much ammunition there was left in the depots. So there's the chief of artillery, and in the operative zone in the Main Staff who takes care about that, and of course he reports on the situation either to me or somebody else in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: How many munitions left and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And on the same topic, the next exhibit is P04520, 4520.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, if I look at the document, I see that the -- the T-30 tank artillery, some members were injured, and then if you look later it talks about the deployment of weapons. And it would seem that there are other tanks, one in Orlovac. I guess that's where some members were injured. And then you see Kozica, Tepcici, Debelo Brdo, Planinica. So if I understood correctly, there were at least five tanks there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, T-130 is a cannon. It's not a tank; it's a cannon, a gun. And it speaks about military targets here, and also it says that the tank crew, who were quite far off, so the BH Army's artillery -- well, you see the people who were wounded, and there was an exchange of fire between -- and it says at the end Orlovac, which is a 130 cannon, and it says that military targets were observed. So they observed the target. They found the target. They hit the target, and here's what happened. No tanks are mentioned here at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: There is clearly mistake in translation. In Croat language it is written, I am quoting: [Interpretation] "Cannon crew, gun crew, cannon crew." [In English] I am quoting: "The tank crew." This is clearly mistaken in translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In fact, yes, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it says here that Mr. Marko Stojicic was the chief of the -- of the cannon crew and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the exchange of artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, thanks to Mr. Prlic I understand better. When it says T-130, it's a gun and not a tank; whereas in the English version of this report, it said tank crew. But it's a gun, and not a tank.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well. 130 is -- when we see 130, it's 130 millimetres; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is P04520. This one's dated on the following day, the 26th of August, 1993. And this is a report that appears to be signed or made on behalf of the operative zone commander Miljenko Lasic. And in item number 1, he's talking about the operation in Rastani and the use of anti-aircraft defence weapons. And so what he's doing is to describe the firing positions of the anti-aircraft defence weapons used during the operation in Rastani. And then in item number 2, you'll see, he makes a reference to the PAM 14.5 positioned from Crne Stijene towards Kucejko, tasked with firing on Brana and targets in Vrapcici, and support for Tuta's men in the assault operation on Rastani.
